dublinCore.title: Sampling Theorem Explorer
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: Signal Processing
Sampling Theorem
Nyquist Frequency
Aliasing
Signal Reconstruction
dublinCore.description: Sample a sine wave at an adjustable rate and rebuild it from the samples with ideal sinc interpolation, a zero-order hold or linear interpolation. Time plots and a spectrum with the Nyquist frequency marked show why a tone above half the sampling rate folds to a lower alias frequency.

learningObjectives: State the sampling theorem and the meaning of the Nyquist rate and the Nyquist frequency
Predict the alias frequency of an under-sampled tone
Explain aliasing as the overlap of spectral copies created by sampling
Compare ideal sinc reconstruction with zero-order hold and linear interpolation
Relate the heights of the spectral lines under a practical reconstruction to |sinc(f/fs)| and sinc^2(f/fs)
prerequisites: The idea of a frequency spectrum

misconceptions.misconception: Sampling at exactly twice the highest frequency always allows perfect reconstruction
misconceptions.correction: The theorem needs fs strictly greater than 2 fmax; at fs = 2 fmax a zero-phase sine is sampled only at its zero crossings and nothing is recovered
misconceptions.evidence: Set fmax = 25 Hz and fs = 50 Hz: the banner turns red, every sample is zero and the reconstruction is a flat line

misconceptions.misconception: An under-sampled tone simply disappears or turns into noise
misconceptions.correction: It reappears as a clean sine at the alias frequency |fmax - k fs| inside [0, fs/2]
misconceptions.evidence: Set fmax = 40 Hz and fs = 50 Hz: the reconstruction is a 10 Hz sine and the spectrum has a grey copy at 10 Hz inside the shaded band

misconceptions.misconception: Aliasing can be removed by filtering after sampling
misconceptions.correction: The samples of the 40 Hz tone and of an inverted 10 Hz sine are identical, so no processing of the samples can tell them apart; the tone must be removed before the sampler
misconceptions.evidence: At fs = 50 Hz the samples for fmax = 40 Hz are the negatives of the samples for fmax = 10 Hz, so they equal the samples of an inverted 10 Hz sine

accessibility.screenReaderScript: Four plots: a continuous sine wave, its samples, the signal reconstructed from the samples, and the frequency spectrum with the Nyquist frequency marked. A banner states whether the sampling rate is high enough or the tone is aliased to a lower frequency.

controls.label: Signal frequency fmax (Hz)
controls.description: Sets the frequency of the sine wave being sampled

controls.label: Sampling rate fs (Hz)
controls.description: Sets the sampling rate; the Nyquist frequency is fs / 2

controls.label: Reconstruction
controls.description: Chooses how the signal is rebuilt from its samples

controls.label: Show sinc pulses
controls.description: Draws the individual sinc pulses whose sum is the ideal reconstruction; available only with ideal reconstruction

visualElements.description: Three time plots over 200 ms: the continuous signal, its samples and the reconstructed signal with the original dashed
Spectrum from 0 to 200 Hz with spectral copies at k fs +/- fmax, the Nyquist band, the reconstruction filter gain and the reconstruction output
Banner stating whether fs > 2 fmax, fs = 2 fmax or fs < 2 fmax and the alias frequency

model.description: A zero-phase sine is sampled at fs and rebuilt by sinc interpolation (drawn in closed form as the sine at the folded frequency), a zero-order hold or linear interpolation
equations: alias frequency = |fmax - k fs|, k = round(fmax / fs)
x_r(t) = sum over n of x[n] sinc((t - n Ts) / Ts)
zero-order hold gain = |sinc(f / fs)|, linear interpolation gain = sinc^2(f / fs)

variables.name: fmax
variables.description: Frequency of the sampled tone in hertz

variables.name: alias
variables.description: Frequency of the reconstructed tone in [0, fs/2]

instructionalStrategies: Predict-then-verify the alias frequency before reading the banner
Lower the sampling rate step by step and record where reconstruction fails
Compare the spectral lines of the zero-order hold and linear interpolation
extensions: Add a second tone and show that two aliases can land on the same frequency
Add an anti-aliasing filter before the sampler
